sections.heading: Asking you to tear down my pride
sections.text: God, every good thing comes from you. Please go after the pride in me that still wants to stand tall without you. Tear down the thoughts that make me feel above correction. Strip away every scrap of self-righteousness I cling to. Give me a low and honest heart before you—not fake humility, but true repentance. Let me see my sin clearly enough to grieve it, and let that grief lead me back to you. Break what needs to be broken in me, and then heal me with your own hands.
theological_themes: God is the source of all goodness; pride and self-righteousness must be exposed and destroyed; true repentance includes grief over sin and dependence on God's mercy.

scripture_references.connection: David shows that God receives a broken and contrite heart, not religious performance or self-protection. This supports the prayer’s request for honest repentance rather than prideful self-justification.
Jesus contrasts the self-righteous Pharisee with the tax collector who simply asks for mercy. The prayer’s desire to be stripped of self-righteousness follows the same gospel logic.
Paul rejects righteousness of his own and wants to be found in Christ. That directly grounds the prayer’s request that every clinging shred of self-righteousness be removed.

sections.heading: Becoming a home for you
sections.text: Make my heart ready for you to live in me. Father, make your home with me. Lord Jesus, come near with the healing only you can give. Holy Spirit, come and make me holy from the inside out. Holy Trinity—Father, Son, and Spirit, one God—take possession of me. Let my life be a place set apart for your glory.
theological_themes: The triune God dwells with and in his people; Christ heals; the Spirit sanctifies; the believer belongs to God as a consecrated dwelling place.

scripture_references.connection: Jesus promises that the Father and Son will make their home with the one who loves him. This supports the prayer’s request for God’s personal indwelling presence.
Paul teaches that believers are temples of the Holy Spirit and belong to God. That grounds the prayer’s language of being consecrated for God’s glory.
Paul blesses the church in the grace of Christ, the love of God, and the fellowship of the Holy Spirit. This reflects the explicitly Trinitarian shape of the prayer.

sections.heading: Trusting what your presence brings
sections.text: When you are with me, sin cannot be treated as a welcome guest. In fellowship with you there is deep joy. Under your kindness my conscience can rest. Close to you, I do not have to be ruled by fear or anxious imagining. Make my heart alive again, like something growing and fragrant because it is near the light. Bring me through repentance into the kind of life where your presence is welcomed, not resisted.
theological_themes: God’s presence drives out cherished evil, brings joy and peace, quiets fear, and renews the believer’s inner life through repentance.

scripture_references.connection: The psalm connects God’s presence with fullness of joy and lasting pleasure. This supports the prayer’s confidence that fellowship with God is the place of true gladness.

John refuses the idea that someone can enjoy fellowship with God while walking in darkness, and he calls believers to confession and cleansing. This grounds the prayer’s desire for repentance that welcomes God’s presence.
Paul teaches believers to bring anxiety to God in prayer and receive God’s guarding peace. This illuminates the prayer’s movement from fear and unrest into peace before God.

sections.heading: Remembering how great you are
sections.text: There is nothing beyond your power. Nothing is too hard for you to do, and nothing good is beyond your willingness to give. Your strength has no limit. Your love is deeper than I can measure. Your grace is more generous than I can understand. Your saving name is glorious. So I do not want to pray small, unbelieving prayers to a great God.
theological_themes: God is omnipotent, loving, gracious, and mighty to save; faith asks boldly because God’s greatness exceeds human limits.

scripture_references.connection: Paul praises God as able to do far more abundantly than believers ask or think, for his glory in the church and in Christ. This supports the prayer’s confidence in asking great things from a great God.
Jeremiah confesses that the Lord made heaven and earth by his power and that nothing is too hard for him. This directly grounds the prayer’s appeal to God’s limitless ability.

sections.heading: Asking you to do saving work everywhere
sections.text: Let heaven rejoice over sinners who turn back to you. Bring home people who have wandered far. Restore those who have drifted and fallen back. Free people held captive by Satan’s lies and power. Open blind eyes. Bind up broken hearts. Encourage the crushed and hopeless. Strip self-righteous people of their false confidence. Drive religious people out of hiding places built on lies. Teach the ignorant the truth. Strengthen your people and build them up in the faith. Great God, I am asking you for great mercy and great rescue, because that is the kind of God you are.
theological_themes: God saves, restores, delivers, enlightens, comforts, humbles, and builds up his people; the church’s hope for sinners rests in God’s great mercy and power.

scripture_references.connection: Jesus says heaven rejoices over one sinner who repents. This supports the prayer’s desire that angels celebrate repentant sinners and restored wanderers.
Paul’s commission includes opening eyes, turning people from darkness to light, and from Satan’s power to God. This closely matches the prayer’s pleas for release from captivity and enlightenment.

Isaiah speaks of good news for the poor, liberty for captives, and comfort for mourners, a passage Jesus applies to his own ministry. It grounds the prayer’s requests for healing, freedom, and comfort for the brokenhearted.
Jude calls believers to be built up in the faith and kept in God’s love. This supports the prayer’s closing request that saints be strengthened in holy faith.

content_provenance.original_author: Unattributed Puritan source (compiled and edited by Arthur Bennett)
content_provenance.original_source: The Valley of Vision: A Collection of Puritan Prayers and Devotions, ed. Arthur Bennett (The Banner of Truth Trust)
content_provenance.source_copyright_status: Compilation, titles and arrangement in copyright (Banner of Truth, 1975); underlying Puritan sources are public domain.
content_provenance.modern_version_note: Contemporary prayer based on the theological themes and ideas of the historical source; not a reproduction of the original wording.

theological_issues_identified: The original uses very severe language about self-loathing and self-abhorrence. I preserved its theological force as hatred of sin and rejection of self-righteousness, while avoiding wording that could be misread as denying the dignity of a person made in God’s image and redeemed in Christ.

The line asking God to make the believer 'meet, through repentance, for thine indwelling' could sound as though repentance earns God’s presence. I rendered it as repentance making the heart welcoming rather than resistant, while keeping the original’s seriousness about sin and holiness.

The prayer’s Trinitarian indwelling language is rich but needs care: the Father, Son, and Spirit are not three separate gods taking turns, but the one God personally present with his people. The adaptation explicitly names the Holy Trinity as one God.
significant_interpretive_choices: I interpreted 'break me, then bind me up' as God’s loving work of conviction and healing, not as punishment for its own sake.

I rendered 'formalist driven from a refuge of lies' as religious people being driven out of hiding places built on lies, meaning outward religion used as false security rather than true faith and repentance.

I treated the closing list as a broad prayer for God’s saving and restoring work among many kinds of people, not merely as private self-examination, because the original widens from the individual heart to God’s work in sinners, prodigals, backsliders, captives, and saints.
